title: Cover-time robustness can stay positive while hitting-time robustness vanishes
shortTitle: Random walks: robust to cover, fragile to hit
oneLine: On a huge clique with a private leaf on every vertex and one extra path of length L, an adversary nudging transition probabilities can be tolerated up to a fixed ε ≈ 0.293 before cover time doubles, but only ε ≈ 0.628/L before hitting time doubles, refuting Zuckerman's conjecture that the two tolerances always agree up to a constant.
abstract: A random walk explores a network by moving to a uniformly chosen neighbour at each step. The hitting time is the expected time to reach one given vertex in the worst case; the cover time is the expected time to visit every vertex. Zuckerman (Markov Chain Robustness, ITCS 2026) asked how much an adversary who may change each transition probability by a relative factor between 1−ε and 1+ε, with history-dependent choices, can slow these quantities down, and conjectured (Conjecture 1.17) that the largest tolerable ε for hitting time and for cover time always agree up to a constant factor. This candidate refutes that conjecture with sharp limiting tolerances. Take a complete graph on N = 2^(2^L) vertices, attach a private leaf to each vertex and attach one extra path of length L. For every fixed amplification budget C > 1, the hitting-time tolerance satisfies Lρ_hit → a_C, where (e^(2a_C)−1)/(2a_C) = C, because a small bias compounds along the path; the cover-time tolerance tends to min{1−C^(−1/2), 1/3} > 0, because collecting the leaves dominates and an adversary can inflate it only by (1−ε)^(−2). For C = 2 these are about 0.628/L and 0.293, and the ratio grows like log log |V|. The paper also proves a uniform cover-response formula, the exact critical multiplier 9/4 + 9/(8 log 2) ≈ 3.873 and tolerance expansions through order 1/L. The graphs have unbounded degree and are astronomically large: the theorem is asymptotic, and bounded-degree versions remain open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Hitting-time robustness vanishes (Theorem 1.1): on G_L, a clique on N = 2^(2^L) vertices with a private leaf on each vertex and one path of length L, L·ρ_hit(G_L;C) → a_C for every fixed budget C > 1, where (e^(2a_C)−1)/(2a_C) = C; for C = 2, a_2 ≈ 0.628.

Cover-time robustness stays positive (Theorem 1.1): ρ_cov(G_L;C) → min{1−C^(−1/2), 1/3} > 0; for C = 2 this is 1 − 1/√2 ≈ 0.293. Below ε = 1/3 the worst cover-time multiplier tends to (1−ε)^(−2); above it, to infinity.

Conjecture 1.17 fails (Theorem 1.1): ρ_cov/ρ_hit grows like a constant times L, that is Θ(log log |V|), for every fixed pair of hitting and cover budgets; this is consistent with Zuckerman's Theorem 1.15 because t_cov/(t_hit log|V|) → 0 here.

Uniform response and critical window (Theorem 1.2, Section 9): t⁺_cov/(N² log N) = a_ε + b e^(−a_ε/b) + O(1/log N) uniformly in ε, with exact critical multiplier 9/4 + 9/(8 log 2) ≈ 3.873 at ε = 1/3, and cover-tolerance expansions through order 1/L for every budget.

Scope: unbounded degree and astronomically large graphs; bounded-degree and regular versions, the converse comparison, the largest possible separation and the strong-adversary cover tolerance remain open.

narration: Can a random walk be robust for one job and fragile for another? An Evidence Press briefing. Picture a walker exploring a network, at each step moving to a randomly chosen neighbour. Two classic measures say how long exploration takes. The hitting time is how long it takes to reach one particular place. The cover time is how long it takes to visit everywhere. In a paper presented in 2026, David Zuckerman asked what happens when an adversary may nudge every step's probabilities up or down by a small relative amount, called epsilon, choosing with full knowledge of the past. How large can epsilon be before the walk slows down by more than a fixed factor? He conjectured that the answer is always about the same for hitting and for covering. This paper shows that it is not. The example is a huge cluster in which every point is joined to every other, each point also has its own private dead end, and one long thin path hangs off the side. Reaching the far end of that path is fragile: a tiny consistent push away from it compounds along every step, so the tolerable epsilon shrinks like one over the path's length. Covering the whole network is different. Most of the work is collecting all the private dead ends, and the adversary can only inflate that cost by a bounded factor. So the tolerable epsilon for covering stays fixed. For a slowdown budget of two, covering tolerates about zero point two nine, while hitting tolerates about zero point six three divided by the path length. The paper also finds the exact slowdown at the tipping point, about three point eight seven. There are limits. The networks are astronomically large, so this is a statement about limits, not practical sizes. Their points have huge numbers of neighbours, so the question for networks with few neighbours per point stays open, as do several related questions. The computer checks are small supporting tests, not the proof. A companion release answers a different question from the same paper, about distance and hitting time. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the fourth of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and code are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Whether the perturbation tolerances that keep hitting time and cover time within a constant factor always agree up to constants (Zuckerman's Conjecture 1.17): no, they can differ by a factor of order log log |V|.
decisionObject.scope: Connected simple graphs with the standard relative-error adversary; the explicit family has unbounded degree and N = 2^(2^L) core vertices; bounded-degree graphs and the strong adversary are excluded.
